source_text: Ecce idem Moyses refert alio in loco, quod Abrahae uisus sit deus. quod nemo hominum deum uideat et utuat. potest deus, quomodo uisus est deus? quomodo uideri non potest? inquit, wdit umguam; hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. mentitur; ergo uere uisus est deus. ex quo intellegi potest, quod non pater uisus sit, qui numquam uisus est, sed filius, qui et descendere solitus est, et uideri quia descenderit. imago ro est enim éinuisibilis dei, ut mediocritas et fragilitas condicionis humanae deum patrem uidere aliquando iam tunc assuesceret in imagine dei, hoc est, in filio dei. gradatim enim et per incrementa fragilitas humana nutriri debuit per imaginem ad istam gloriam, ut deum patrem uidere possit aliquando, periculosa sunt enim quae magna sunt, si repentina sunt. nam etiam lux solis subita post tenebras splendore nimio insuetis oculis non ostendet diem, sed potius faciet caecitatem. quod ne in damnum humanorum contingat oculorum, paulatim disruptis et dissipatis tenebris, ortus luminaris istius mediocribus incrementis fallenter assurgens oculos hominum sensim assuefacit ad totum orbem suum ferendum per incrementa radiorum. sic ergo et Christus, id est imago dei et filius dei, ab hominibus inspicitur, qua poterat uideri. et ideo fragilitas et mediocritas sortis humanae per ipsum alitur, producitur, educatur, ut aliquando deum quoque ipsum patrem, assueta filium conspicere, possit, w est, uidere; ne maiestatis ipsius repentino et intolerabili fulgore percussa intercipi possit, ut deum patrem quem semper optauit uidere non possit. ex quo filius est hic qui uidetur; dei autem filius, dei uerbum est; dei autem uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. quae, malum, ratio est ut dubitetur deus dici, qui tot modis deus intellegitur approbari? Ac si et Agar ancillam Sarae de domo eiectam pariter et fugatam angelus conuenit apud fontem aquae in uia Sur, fugae causas interrogat atque accipit, et post haec humilitatis consilia porrigit, spem praeterea illi materni nominis facit, quodque ex utero eius multum semen esset futurum spondet atque promittit, et quod Hismael ex illa nasci haberet, et cum ceteris aperit locum habitationis ipsius, actumque describit: hunc autem angelum et dominum scriptura proponit et deum (nam nec benedictionem seminis promisisset, nisi angelus et deus fuisset): quaerant quid in praesenti loco haeretici tractent. - pater fuit iste qui ab Agar uisus est, an non? quia deus positus sed absit deum patrem angelum dicere; ne alteri subsed angelum dicent fuisse. quomodo ergo deus erit, si angelus fuit, cum non sit hoc nomen angelis umquam concessum? nisi quoniam ex utroque latere nos ueritas in istam concludit sententiam, qua intellegere debeamus dei filium fuisse: qui, quoniam ex deo est, merito deus, quia dei filius, dictus sit, quoniam patri subditus et annuntiator paternae uoluntatis est, magni consilii angelus pronuntiatus est. ergo si hic locus neque personae patris congruit, ne angelus dictus sit, neque personae angeli, ne, deus pronuntiatus sit; personae autem Christi conuenit ut et deus sit, quia dei filius est, et angelus sit, quoniam paternae dispositionis annuntiator est: intellegere debent contra scripturas se agere haeretici, qui Christum cum dicant se et angelum credere, nolint illum etiam deum pronuntiare, quem in ueteri testamento ad uisitationem generis humani legunt\ saepe uenisse. Adhuc adiecit Moyses, Abrahae uisum deum apud quercum Mambre, sedente ipso ad ostium tabernaculi sui meridie, et nihilominus, cum tres conspexisset uiros, unum ex illis dominum nuncupasse; quorum cum pedes lauisset, cinericios panes cum butyro et ipsius copia lactis offert, et ut hospites retenti uescerentur, hortatur. post quae et quod pater futurus esset, audit; et quod Sara uxor eius paritura ex ipso filium esset, ediscit; et de exitu Sodomitarum, quae merebantur pati, recognoscit; et quod propter clamorem Sodomorum deus descendisset, addiscit. quo in loco si patrem uolunt uideri tunc fuisse cum angelis duobus hospitio receptum, patrem uisibilem haeretici crediderunt: si autem angelum, cum ex angelis tribus unus dominus nuncupatur, cur, quod non solet, angelus deus dicitur? nisi quoniam, ut deo patri inuisibilitas propria reddatur, et angelo propria mediocritas remittatur, non nisi dei filius, qui et deus est, Abrahae uisus et hospitio receptus esse credetur. quod enim erat futurus, meditabatur in sacramento Abrahae factus hospes, apud Abrahae filios futurus; cuius filiorum pedes, ad probationem quod ipse esset, abluit; reddens in filiis ius hospitalitatis, quod aliquando illi fenerauerat pater. unde et ne qua esset dubitatio quin iste Abrahae hospes fuisset, in Sodomitarum exitu ponitur: quoniam pluit dominus super Sodomam et Gomorram ignem et sulphur a domino de caelo. sic enim et prophetes ex persona dei: subuerti uos, inquit, sécut subuertit dominus Sodomam et Gomorram. dominus ergo Sodomam subuertit, id est, deus Sodomam subuertit: sed.in subuersione Sodomorum dominus pluit ignem a domino. hic autem dominus uisus est Abrahae deus: deus autem hic hospes est Abrahae uisus utique quia tactus. sed cum pater, quia inuisibilis, nec tunc utique uisus sit, uisus est et hospitio receptus et acceptus est, qui solitus est tangi et uideri: hic autem filius dei dominus a domino pluit super Sodomam et Gomorram sulphur atque ignem. hic autem dei uerbum est: uerbum autem dei caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. non pater igitur apud Abraham hospes, sed Christus fuit; nec tunc pater uisus est, sed filius; uisus autem est Christus. merito igitur Christus et dominus et deus est, qui non aliter Abrahae uisus est, nisi quia ante ipsum Abraham ex patre deo deus sermo generatus est. Adhuc, inquit, idem angelus et deus eandem Agar, fugatam de domo Abrahae cum puero, consolatur et uisitat. nam cum illa in solitudine exposuisset infantem, quia aqua defecisset ex utre, cumque puer ille clamasset, fletum et planctum leuasset, et audiuit, inquit scriptura, deus uocem pueri ae loco ubi erat. cum deum esse, qui uocem audisset infantis, rettulisset, adiecit: et uocauit angelus domini ipsam Agar de caelo; angelum referens esse quem deum dixerat, et~dominum pronuntians esse quem angelum collocarat.. quique angelus et deus adhuc ipsi Agar promittit maiora solacia, dicendo: ne timueris; exaudiui enim uocem pueri de loco ubi erat. surge, sume puerum, et tene: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum. hic angelus, si angelus tantum est, cur hoc sibi uindicat ut dicat: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum, cum hoc utique genus potentiae dei sit, angeli esse non possit? ex quo etiam deus confirmatur esse qui hoc potest facere. quoniam ut hoc ipsum comprobetur, adicitur per scripturam statim: e aperuit deus oculos eius, et uidit puteum aquae uiuae, et abiit, et impleuit utrem de puteo, et dedit puero, et erat deus cum puero. si ergo hic deus erat cum puero, qui aperuit oculos Agar, ut uideret puteum aquae uiuae et hauriret aquam propter urgentem sitis necessitatem; hic autem deus e caelo illam uocat; angelus dictus, cum superius uocem audiens clamantis pueri deus esset potius, non alius intellegitur quam angelus esse pariter et deus. quod cum patri competens et conueniens esse non possit, qui tantummodo deus est, competens autem esse possit Christo, qui non tantummodo deus sed et angelus pronuntiatus est, manifeste apparet non patrem ibi tunc locutum fuisse ad Agar, sed Christum potius, cum deus sit, cui etiam angeli competit nomen, quippe cum magni consili angelus factus sit; angelus autem sit, dum exponit sinum patris, sicut Ioannes edicit. si enim ipse Ioannes hunc eundem, qui sinum exponit patris, uerbum dicit carnem factum esse, ut sinum patris posset exponere, merito Christus non solum homo est, sed et angelus; nec angelus tantum, sed et deus per scripturas ostenditur, et a nobis hoc esse creditur, ne, si non Christum tunc locutum ad Agar uoluerimus accipere, aut angelum deum faciamus, aut deum patrem omnipotentem inter angelos computemus.
pass_a_gloss: Behold, Moses reports in another place that God was seen by Abraham. That no man of men sees God and lives. How can God be seen? How can He not be seen? He says, 'No man has ever seen Him'; no man of men can see Him. He lies; therefore, God was truly seen. From which it can be understood that it was not the Father who was seen, who was never seen, but the Son, who was accustomed to descend and be seen because He had descended. For the image of the invisible God is the Son, so that the mediocrity and fragility of the human condition might become accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God, that is, in the Son of God. For human fragility had to be nourished gradually and through increments to this glory, so that it might be able to see God the Father someday, for great things are dangerous if they are sudden. For even the light of the sun, after darkness, does not show the day to unaccustomed eyes with too much splendor, but rather causes blindness. So that this might not happen to the detriment of human eyes, with the darkness gradually broken and dispersed, the rising of this luminary, slowly and gently ascending, accustoms human eyes to bear its entire orb through the increments of its rays. So also Christ, that is, the image of God and the Son of God, is seen by men, insofar as He can be seen. And therefore, the fragility and mediocrity of the human lot are nourished, produced, and educated through Him, so that someday, having become accustomed to seeing the Son, it might be able to see God the Father Himself; that is, see Him, lest it be struck by the sudden and intolerable splendor of His majesty and be unable to see God the Father, whom it had always desired to see. From which it follows that the Son is the one who is seen; but the Son of God is the Word of God; and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelled among us: this is Christ. What evil reasoning is it to doubt that He is called God, who is approved as God in so many ways? And if the angel met Hagar, the servant of Sarah, who was cast out and fled from her home, at the spring of water on the road to Shur, and asked about the reasons for her flight, and received them, and after these things gave her counsel of humility, and also gave her hope of the name of mother, and promised that there would be a great multitude of offspring from her, and that Ishmael would be born from her, and showed her the place of his habitation, and described his actions: let the heretics examine what is being treated in this present passage. Was it the Father who was seen by Hagar, or not? Because God is spoken of, but it is absurd to say that God the Father is an angel; lest they say that another angel was present. How, then, can He be God if He was an angel, since this name is never given to angels? Unless, indeed, the truth from both sides concludes us to this sentence, that we ought to understand it to be the Son of God: who, because He is from God, is rightly called God, because He is the Son of God, and is called the angel of great counsel, because He is subject to the Father and announces the Father's will. Therefore, if this passage does not fit the person of the Father, lest He be called an angel, nor the person of an angel, lest He be called God; but fits the person of Christ, that He is both God, because He is the Son of God, and an angel, because He is the announcer of the Father's disposition: the heretics ought to understand that they are acting against the Scriptures, who say they believe Christ to be an angel, but do not want to pronounce Him to be God, whom they read in the Old Testament to have come often to visit the human race. Moreover, Moses added that God was seen by Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while he was sitting at the door of his tent at noon, and nonetheless, when he saw three men, he called one of them Lord; and when he washed their feet, he offered them ashes and bread with butter, and an abundance of milk, and urged them to eat as retained guests. After these things, he heard that he would be a father; and that Sarah, his wife, would bear a son from him, he learned; and about the destruction of the Sodomites, who deserved to suffer, he recognized; and that God had descended because of the cry of the Sodomites, he learned. In this place, if they want the Father to have been seen then with the two angels who were received as guests, the heretics have believed in a visible Father: but if it was an angel, since one of the three angels is called Lord, why is an angel called God, which is not usual? Unless, indeed, in order that the invisibility proper to God the Father might be preserved, and the mediocrity proper to an angel might be remitted, it is believed that the Son of God, who is also God, was seen by Abraham and received as a guest. For what was going to happen, He was meditating in the sacrament, having become a guest with Abraham, and was going to be with the sons of Abraham; whose feet, as a proof that He Himself was, He washed; rendering in the sons the right of hospitality, which the Father had once rendered to Him. Whence also, lest there be any doubt that this guest of Abraham was He, it is placed in the destruction of the Sodomites: because the Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord in heaven. For thus also the prophets speak in the person of God: 'I will overturn you', He says, 'as the Lord overturned Sodom and Gomorrah.' Therefore, the Lord overturned Sodom, that is, God overturned Sodom: but in the overturning of the Sodomites, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. But this Lord was seen by Abraham as God; and God is this guest who was seen by Abraham, certainly because He was touched. But since the Father, because He is invisible, was not seen then, He who is accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received as a guest: this Lord, however, is the Son of God, who rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord. But this is the Word of God: and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelled among us: this is Christ. Therefore, it was not the Father who was a guest with Abraham, but Christ; and it was not the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Therefore, Christ is rightly Lord and God, who was seen by Abraham in no other way than because, before Him, Abraham was generated from God the Father as God the Word. Moreover, it is said that the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar, who was cast out from Abraham's home with her son. For when she had exposed the infant in the wilderness, because the water had failed from the skin, and the boy had cried out, and had raised weeping and lamentation, and He heard, as Scripture says, the voice of the boy from the place where he was. When He had reported that it was God who had heard the voice of the infant, He added: and the angel of the Lord called her, Hagar, from heaven; referring to the angel as the one whom He had called God, and pronouncing Him to be Lord whom He had placed as an angel. And this angel and God promised greater solaces to Hagar, saying: 'Do not fear; for I have heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was. Rise, take the boy, and hold him; for I will make him a great nation.' This angel, if he is only an angel, why does he claim this for himself, saying: 'I will make him a great nation', since this is a kind of power that belongs to God, and cannot belong to an angel? From which it is also confirmed that He is God, who can do this. For in order that this very thing might be proven, it is added through Scripture immediately: and God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water, and she went and filled the skin from the well, and gave it to the boy, and God was with the boy. If, then, this was God who was with the boy, who opened Hagar's eyes, so that she might see the well of living water and draw water because of the urgent necessity of thirst; and this God called her from heaven; and the angel is spoken of, since, above, He was hearing the voice of the crying boy as God rather than another, it is understood that He is not other than the angel and God. Which, since it is fitting and suitable for the Father, who is only God, and cannot be suitable, but can be suitable for Christ, who is not only God but also pronounced to be an angel, it clearly appears that it was not the Father who spoke to Hagar then, but rather Christ, since He is God, to whom the name of angel is also suitable, since He was made the angel of great counsel; and He is an angel, since He reveals the bosom of the Father, as John testifies. For if John himself says that this same one, who reveals the bosom of the Father, is the Word made flesh, so that He might reveal the bosom of the Father, it is right that Christ is not only man, but also angel; and not only angel, but also God, as is shown through the Scriptures, and is believed by us, lest, if we do not want to accept that Christ spoke to Hagar then, we either make an angel God, or count God the Father among the angels.

pass_b_english: Moses reports elsewhere that God appeared to Abraham, even though no human being can see God and live. How can God be seen if no one has ever seen Him or is able to see Him? The claim that God was seen would be a lie—unless it was truly God who appeared. From this we understand that the one seen was not the Father, who has never been seen, but the Son, who is accustomed to descend and to be seen precisely because He has descended. He is the image of the invisible God, given so that the frailty and limitation of our human condition might gradually become accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God, that is, in the Son of God (John 1:14). Human weakness had to be nurtured step by step toward that glory, so that it might someday be able to see the Father; for great things are dangerous when they come suddenly. Even the sun's light, bursting forth after darkness, does not reveal the day to unaccustomed eyes but blinds them instead. To prevent such damage to human eyes, the rising of this heavenly light ascends gently, its rays increasing little by little, accustoming our vision to bear its full brilliance. In the same way Christ, the image and Son of God, is seen by human beings insofar as He can be seen. Through Him our frailty is nourished, developed, and trained, so that—once accustomed to seeing the Son—we may someday see God the Father Himself, and not be struck down by the sudden, intolerable splendor of His majesty, which would rob us of the vision we have always longed for. Therefore the one seen is the Son; the Son of God is the Word of God; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and this is Christ (John 1:14). What perverse reasoning doubts that He should be called God, when He is attested as God in so many ways?

Consider Hagar, Sarah's servant, cast out and fleeing. An angel met her at a spring on the road to Shur, questioned her about her flight, gave her counsel of humility, promised her the name "mother" and a multitude of descendants through Ishmael, and showed her where he would dwell (Genesis 16:7-14). Scripture calls this figure both angel and Lord and God—for He would not have promised the blessing of seed unless He were both angel and God. Let heretics examine who is at work here. Was it the Father whom Hagar saw? God is named, but it is absurd to call the Father an angel, lest they invent a second angel. How can He be God if He is an angel, since the name "God" is never given to angels? Unless the truth from both sides compels the conclusion that this is the Son of God: because He is from God He is rightly called God; because He is the Son He is called the Angel of Great Counsel, since He is subject to the Father and announces the Father's will (Isaiah 9:6). This passage fits neither the Father (lest He be called an angel) nor a mere angel (lest he be called God); it fits Christ, who is both God as the Son of God and angel as the announcer of the Father's purpose. Heretics who confess Christ as an angel yet refuse to call Him God act against the Scriptures, which record His frequent visits to humanity in the Old Testament.

Moses adds that God appeared to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre while he sat at his tent door at noon. Abraham saw three men, called one of them Lord, washed their feet, and set before them bread, butter, and abundant milk, urging them to eat as guests (Genesis 18:1). Afterwards he heard that he would become a father, that Sarah would bear a son, and learned of the coming destruction of the Sodomites and that God had descended because of their outcry. If heretics insist the Father was seen there alongside two angels, they make the Father visible. But if it was an angel, why is one of the three called Lord and addressed as God—something never done for a mere angel? The only coherent explanation is that the Son of God, who is also God, appeared to Abraham and was received as a guest, preserving the Father's invisibility and the angel's proper mediocrity. He was anticipating, in a sacramental sign, His future dwelling among Abraham's descendants; He washed their feet as proof of who He was, returning in the sons the right of hospitality the Father had once extended to Him. Lest any doubt remain that this guest was He, the account continues with the destruction of Sodom: the Lord rained fire and sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord in heaven (Genesis 19:24). The prophets speak in God's person: "I will overthrow you as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah" (Amos 4:11). Thus the Lord overthrew Sodom—that is, God overthrew Sodom—yet in that overthrow the Lord rained fire from the Lord. This Lord whom Abraham saw and touched was God; the Father, being invisible, was not seen. The one seen and received, the one accustomed to be touched and seen, is the Son of God, who rained fire from the Lord. He is the Word of God; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; this is Christ (John 1:14). So it was not the Father who was Abraham's guest, but Christ; not the Father who was seen, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Rightly, then, Christ is Lord and God, seen by Abraham in no other way than as the Word, God from God, begotten of the Father before all time.

Again, the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar after she was cast out with her boy. When the water ran out and the child cried, God heard the boy's voice from where he lay (Genesis 16:7-14). Scripture first says God heard; then it says the angel of the Lord called to Hagar from heaven—identifying the angel as the one just called God, and calling Him Lord whom it had just called angel. This angel and God promises greater comfort: "Do not fear; I have heard the boy's voice. Rise, take him, hold him; I will make him a great nation." If this figure is only an angel, how can he claim the divine prerogative of making a great nation? That power belongs to God alone, confirming that He is God. To prove the point, Scripture immediately adds: God opened Hagar's eyes, she saw a well of living water, filled the skin, gave the boy drink, and God was with the boy (Genesis 16:7-14). The same God who opened her eyes called her from heaven; the one called angel is the same one who, moments before, heard the boy's cry as God. This identity cannot belong to the Father, who is only God and never appears; but it fits Christ, who is not only God but also designated Angel, since He is the Angel of Great Counsel and reveals the Father's bosom, as John testifies (John 1:18). John says the Word made flesh is the one who reveals the Father's bosom. Therefore Christ is not only man, but also angel; not only angel, but also God, as Scripture demonstrates and we believe—lest, refusing to accept that Christ spoke to Hagar, we either make a mere angel into God or count the Almighty Father among the angels.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments of Novatian regarding the visibility of the Son versus the invisibility of the Father. All scripture citations in Pass B (John 1:14, Genesis 16:7-14, Isaiah 9:6, Genesis 18:1, Genesis 19:24, Amos 4:11, John 1:18) correctly identify the biblical passages alluded to in the Latin text. The distinction between the 'angel' and 'God' in the Hagar and Abraham passages is preserved. Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source.
